seo as part of digital marketing
h1: Where SEO fits inside digital marketing
metaTitle: What Is SEO in Digital Marketing? Where It Fits
metaDescription: What is SEO in digital marketing? The channel that captures existing demand. Here's how it works alongside ads, social and email, not against them.
answer: Inside digital marketing, SEO is the demand-capture channel: it puts you in front of people already searching for what you sell. Social, PR and display create demand; search captures it. That's the division of labour, and it's why SEO's cost per lead falls over time while paid channels' rises with competition.
takeaways: Search is the only channel where the customer starts the conversation. Everything else interrupts someone doing something else.
SEO captures demand. Social and PR create it. A plan with only one of the two either runs out of buyers or never reaches them.
Paid search is SEO's cheapest research tool — it tells you which keywords convert in three weeks instead of nine months.
Budget split should move with stage, not with fashion. Early on, weight paid. As CAC rises, weight organic.

sections.h2: SEO's actual job in the mix
body: Digital marketing is usually taught as a list of channels — SEO, PPC, social, email, affiliates, content — which tells you what exists and nothing about how they relate. The useful split is by what each does to demand.

SEO's job is capture. Someone has already decided they have a problem, typed it into a search box, and the only question is whether you're one of the options they see. You didn't create that intent. You met it.

That single fact explains most of SEO's economics. Search traffic converts better per visit than almost anything else, because the visitor arrived with a question rather than being interrupted mid-scroll. It also explains SEO's ceiling: if two hundred people a month search your commercial terms in India, page one for all of them is worth exactly two hundred people a month, no matter how good the agency is.

So SEO isn't a growth engine on its own. It's the collection mechanism sitting under everything else you do — including your offline advertising, your conference booth, and the podcast someone heard you on.
Sort every channel by this one question — does it meet intent or manufacture it — and the plan almost writes itself.

callout.title: The diagnostic
callout.body: If your search volume is flat but your conversion rate is fine, you have a demand-creation problem and more SEO won't fix it. If search volume is healthy and you're invisible for it, that's an SEO problem and more ads are just renting the answer.

sections.h2: The handoffs that make every channel cheaper
body: Channels are usually run as separate line items by separate people who meet monthly. The money is in the handoffs between them, and those are the first thing to break when SEO is outsourced to an agency that never sees the ad account.

subs.h3: Paid search → SEO: which keywords actually convert
body: The most valuable handoff in digital marketing and the most commonly wasted. Your Google Ads search-terms report holds real conversion data against real queries — not a tool's volume estimate. Three weeks of spend tells you which phrases produce enquiries and which produce tyre-kickers.

Feed that list into the content plan and you skip most of the guesswork that makes year one of SEO expensive. The corollary is uncomfortable: if a keyword doesn't convert on paid, it will not convert on organic either. It'll just take you nine months to find out.

subs.h3: SEO → paid search: spend less on the same clicks
bullets: Once a page ranks in the top three organically, you can usually cut or pause paid bids on that exact term and watch what happens to total leads. Sometimes you keep both. Often you free up budget.
Organic query data reveals negative keywords — the irrelevant phrases you're currently paying for. That's a direct, same-month saving.
Landing pages built and tested for SEO usually make better ad destinations than the ones an agency built for the ad, because they answer more of the question.

subs.h3: Social and PR → links, which is half of off-page SEO
body: Links can't be bought safely, so they have to be earned, and the things that earn them are the things PR and social teams already do: original data, a strong opinion published under a real name, a founder saying something quotable, a product launch that journalists cover.

Run those functions in separate silos and you get a PR team generating coverage with no links and an SEO team buying guest posts. Run them together and the same activity does both jobs. See [guest posting vs digital PR](/compare/guest-posting-vs-digital-pr).

subs.h3: SEO → email: capture the 97% who won't buy today
body: Organic traffic arrives with intent, but usually early intent — researching, comparing, not buying yet. Without an email capture, that visit is spent once. With one, it becomes a contact you can reach without paying a platform again. A genuinely useful download on a high-traffic guide typically outperforms the same offer promoted on social, because the reader is already mid-problem.

sections.h2: How the budget should split, by stage
body: There's no universal ratio, and anyone quoting one is guessing. But the direction of travel is consistent: paid-heavy early, organic-heavy as you scale, because paid gets more expensive with competition while organic gets cheaper with accumulation.
Starting points, not laws — adjust for sales cycle, margin, and whether anyone internal can produce content.

callout.title: The most expensive sequencing error
callout.body: Starting SEO before you know what converts. You'll spend six months and several lakh producing content for keywords that bring traffic and no enquiries. Three weeks of paid search would have told you. Run the cheap experiment first.

sections.h2: Where SEO is the wrong first channel
body: SEO is oversold as the default, usually by people who sell it. It genuinely isn't the right opening move in several common situations, and recognising yours saves a year.
bullets: **You need revenue this quarter.** SEO is not a cash-flow instrument. It's an asset build, and assets are paid for before they pay you.
**Nobody searches for your category yet.** New categories need naming before they can be searched. That's a PR and paid-social job first.
**You can't change the website.** Locked template, no developer, no CMS access. Technical fixes are usually the first available return and you can't have them.
**Your product has a six-week shelf life.** Event tickets, seasonal drops, flash inventory. By the time a page ranks, the thing is gone.
**No one internally can feed content.** Agencies without subject-matter input produce the generic pages Google has spent two years demoting.

sections.h2: How to tell whether SEO is under-funded in your mix
body: Six checks. Any two of them coming back badly means the organic side of the plan is starved, not failing.
numbered: **Compare non-branded organic clicks with paid clicks for the same queries.** If you're paying for clicks on terms where you also rank on page two, you're renting something you nearly own.
**Published pages versus indexed pages** in Search Console. A big gap means you're funding production and not fixing the plumbing.
**Referring domains over the last twelve months.** Flat means nobody is doing off-page work, whatever the report says.
**Money-page freshness.** If your service and product pages haven't changed in a year while the blog ships weekly, budget is going to the easy half of the job.
**Cost per lead by channel, trending.** Paid rising while organic stays flat is the moment to shift weight, and most teams notice it two quarters late.

**Share of brand versus non-brand organic.** If nearly all your organic traffic is people typing your name, SEO isn't acquiring anyone — [see how to strip that out of your numbers](/answers/what-is-the-roi-of-seo).

callout.body: SEO from ₹75,000/mo, smaller sites from ₹40,000. SEO plus organic social together is ₹99,000/mo; all three disciplines including performance is ₹1,75,000/mo. Ex-GST, ad spend billed separately with no media markup. [Full pricing](/pricing).

faqs.q: Is SEO part of digital marketing?
faqs.a: Yes — it's one of the core channels, alongside paid search, paid and organic social, email, affiliates and PR. What makes it distinct is that it captures demand rather than creating it: the searcher arrives already looking for what you sell, which is why it converts better per visit than interruptive channels.

faqs.q: What's the difference between SEO and digital marketing?
faqs.a: Digital marketing is the whole set of channels; SEO is one of them. Asking which is better is like asking whether a kitchen is better than a house. The real question is which channel deserves the next rupee, and that depends on whether your bottleneck is people not knowing you exist or people not finding you when they look.

faqs.q: What percentage of a digital marketing budget should go to SEO?
faqs.a: Roughly 10% pre-revenue, rising to 30–40% as customer acquisition costs climb on paid. There's no correct universal figure, and anyone quoting one hasn't looked at your search volume. The signal to shift weight is your paid cost per lead rising while your organic cost per lead stays flat.

faqs.q: Do I need SEO if I'm already running Google Ads?
faqs.a: Usually yes, and the ads make the SEO cheaper. Your search-terms report shows which queries actually convert, so the content plan stops being guesswork. Over time, ranking organically for your best converting terms lets you cut bids on them and put that budget somewhere it's still needed.

faqs.q: How does SEO work with social media?
faqs.a: Social creates demand and familiarity; search captures it. Social links themselves are nofollowed and pass no direct ranking value, but social distribution is how content reaches the journalists, bloggers and operators who do link. Treat social as the distribution layer for the assets SEO needs to earn links.

faqs.q: Which comes first, SEO or paid ads?
faqs.a: Paid, in almost every case where you don't already know what converts. Three weeks of search ads costs less than three months of content and answers a bigger question: whether the demand you're planning to capture actually turns into customers. Then build organically for the terms that passed.
